extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, IP statisticians, researchers, and patent/IP professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, definitions and data-quality notes for interpreting WIPO’s IP and publishing statistics (coverage, inclusion rules, estimation methods and comparability), together with a brief overview of the patent/PCT and related IP systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is granted for an invention that meets the standards of novelty, non-obviousness and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are time-limited exclusive rights (generally 20 years). In return for exclusivity, applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public so that others skilled in the art may replicate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent rights jurisdiction and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the issuing authority and are valid for a limited period (generally 20 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures for acquiring patent rights are governed by national and regional patent offices; applicants must file with a national or regional office to obtain rights in that jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT application process (international and national phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT System facilitates acquisition of patent rights in multiple jurisdictions by an international application that begins with an international phase and concludes with a national phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The international phase includes an international search and optional preliminary examination and supplementary international search. The national phase follows, during which national (or regional) patent offices decide on patentability according to national law. The decision to grant remains the prerogative of national/regional offices. (See www.wipo.int/pct.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model system (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model confers rights to an invention for a limited period, similar to a patent, allowing exclusive commercial exploitation during the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms and conditions of utility model protection vary by jurisdiction; the text notes utility models as a separate IP type analogous to patents (full details appear elsewhere in the report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data interpretation caution (publishing and IP data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution should be exercised when interpreting the data shown here due to data being incomplete and partial. The share of the total publishing industry represented by national publishers’ associations (NPAs) varies between countries. There are also methodological differences that mean it is difficult to make comparisons between countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various figures include footnotes (e.g. * indicates 2018 data). Users should account for incomplete coverage and methodological differences when comparing countries or years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing survey scope and inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO’s global publishing industry survey covers trade and educational publishing only and is limited to published materials that have been issued with an International Standard Book Number (ISBN), a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) or any other national/international book identifier (e.g., ASIN).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2020 edition includes data from 45 associations/authorities for 2019 and nine for 2018. Coverage remains partial and WIPO/IPA plan to improve quality and coverage over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal deposit definition and use in validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal deposit is a statutory obligation at the national level requiring publishers to deposit a certain number of copies of their published documents at a recognized repository (a place of legal deposit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO conducted a pilot legal deposit survey in 2019 (51 responses) and reports 57 authorities in 2020; legal deposit data are used to validate publishing-survey responses. Note: in some countries digital deposits are collected on a voluntary basis (footnotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO IP survey data collection practices
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO collects data from national/regional IP offices, other competent authorities and publishers’ associations through annual surveys consisting of multiple questionnaires; where possible, data published on IP offices’ websites or in annual reports are used to supplement questionnaire responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO’s long-established IP survey covers patents, utility models, trademarks, industrial designs and plant varieties and consists of 28 questionnaires available in English, French and Spanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP offices origin reporting limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: IP offices are requested to report data by the origin (country or territory) of applications, grants or registrations, but some offices cannot provide detailed breakdowns and instead report aggregate totals or simple resident/non-resident counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, totals for each origin are underreported. The report notes unknown-origin shares for 2019 totals are small (e.g., 1.8% for patent applications, 0.5% for trademark application class counts, 0.4% for application design counts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data coverage by IP type (coverage metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The report provides measures of coverage: number of offices on which 2019 world totals are based, number of offices for which 2019 data are available, and data coverage percentage for each IP type (patents, utility models, trademarks, industrial designs, plant varieties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These coverage percentages indicate how much of the estimated world totals are based on reported data (e.g., patents coverage ~99.8%). Users should consult these coverage metrics when assessing reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating world totals methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: World totals of applications and grants/registrations are WIPO estimates: missing data are estimated using methods such as linear extrapolation and averaging adjacent data points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an office provides data not broken down by origin, WIPO estimates resident and non-resident counts using historical shares recorded at that office. The estimation method depends on the year and office; only small shares of world totals are estimated in most cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling breaks in data series (example: CNIPA 2017 change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in an office's counting method can create breaks in time series. Example: CNIPA changed in 2017 from counting all applications received to counting only those for which the office received the necessary application fees; thus data for China in 2017 and 2018 are not comparable with previous years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of such breaks, certain figures do not report 2017 growth and reporting of global growth rates across the break is not meaningful. Users must identify and account for methodological breaks before comparing years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of national and international data inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Application and grant/registration data include both direct filings and filings made through WIPO-administered international systems where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patents and utility models, data comprise direct national filings as well as PCT national phase entries. For trademarks, data comprise national/regional filings and designations received through the Madrid System. For industrial designs, data comprise national/regional applications and designations received through the Hague System.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting conventions for trademarks and industrial designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark application counts are based on class count (the number of classes specified in applications). Industrial design application counts are based on design count (the number of designs contained in applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnotes clarify that some figures refer to class counts or design counts rather than application counts; users should use the appropriate denominators when comparing across IP types or offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of World Bank income classifications and UN regions
rubrics_metrics.description: The report uses the World Bank’s income classifications (2019 gross national income per capita via the World Bank Atlas method) and United Nations definitions of regions and sub-regions for grouping economies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Income class thresholds are provided (low-income ≤ USD 1,035, lower middle USD 1,036–4,045, upper middle USD 4,046–12,535, high-income > USD 12,536). Geographical terms may differ slightly from UN definitions in other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote and time-lag caveats for publishing industry data
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing-industry figures include footnotes such as '*' indicating 2018 data, and several tables warn that national publishers’ association (NPA) coverage varies and methodological differences make cross-country comparisons difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users must check footnotes for time-lagged data (2018 vs 2019) and for country-specific data collection differences (e.g., retail-market values reported for some countries).
